description: Oryx AI — we audit how tightly AI-generated research claims are bound to verifiable evidence. Our Space Apps project harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS fire-hotspot records for Punjab's October 2025 stubble-burning season, measuring what each sensor misses alone.
summary: Two satellites watch the same fires and barely agree — we measured the disagreement and built the burning-activity calendar from the union of both records.
details: Satellites have tracked active fires for over two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly. We tested that claim on real NASA FIRMS data for Punjab, India, in October 2025 — peak stubble-burning season. VIIRS saw 1,902 fires, MODIS saw 927, and only 102 were the same fire seen by both (Jaccard 0.037). MODIS alone would miss more than half the burning season. The reason is in the data: the sensors pass 1–2 hours apart and stubble fires burn for hours, so most fires are genuinely seen by one sensor only — and VIIRS resolves small fires MODIS cannot see. Our web app harmonizes both records into a daily burning-activity calendar for any area of interest, flags the critical periods (18–31 October in Punjab; peak 31 October, 313 detections), and reports the agreement honestly at four matching tolerances so the result cannot be tuned into existence. Built with NASA open data, open source, reproducible from the code in this folder.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS active-fire data, VIIRS S-NPP + MODIS C6.1, India 2025 country archive (Punjab, October 2025)
projectRefs: NASA FIRMS (firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov); method and sources in the project README
